footnote.text: We’re very grateful to you for being here with us, for wasting your life listening to us rambling.

brief.head: Back to school at 30
brief.text: Sayyid Ahmad Khan, founder of Aligarh Muslim University, decided at thirty that he did not know enough, Amit Varma said, and hired six tutors for six subjects. {043-S06}

brief.head: Same tongue, same maps
brief.text: For all the talk of a world changing like never before, Amit Varma said, he still speaks the language he spoke as a child, under the same government and maps. {#samemaps}

brief.head: The plotting poet-king
brief.text: Bahadur Shah Zafar, usually shown as a weak poet-king, was in fact “a schemer and a plotter” who “contained multitudes”, Amit Varma said, drawing on Swapna Liddle. {#zafar}

brief.head: In praise of lust
brief.text: Amit Varma prefers lust to love, because lust is honest. Love, he said, can be a cover for wanting status, social acceptance or companionship with a particular kind of person. {043-C12}

brief.head: Safe in harbour
brief.text: A ship is safe in the harbour, Ajay Shah said, but that is not what ships are for. Germany’s new fleet sat out the First World War in dock. {043-J15}

thought.text: When you write down a word, you ossify it.
thought.who: Amit Varma, on what the printing press did to the languages of Delhi

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah pitch six more films
lead.head: Lights, camera, plutonium
body: Ajay Shah opened by thanking listeners for “wasting your life listening to us rambling”. Amit Varma objected at once. “They’re not wasting their lives,” he said. “We are going to tell them stories.”
It was the hosts’ fourth episode of stories that should be films. Varma brought two fictions and a slice of true history; Shah brought three true tales, the last of them only a scene.
## Into the open sea

Varma’s first pitch grew from a thought experiment by the entrepreneur Deepak VS: replace the IIT entrance exam with a swimming test. By the second year, Deepak warned, Kota would be running swimming classes. {043-C01}
In Varma’s film, a boy who loves engineering is trapped on a treadmill of IIT-sized pools. He finds joy only in the open sea, fails his exam, and swims out past the danger marker into a storm.
Shah called it “a great metaphor for our times”, but asked for a more redemptive story. “Redemption, you want a happy story,” Varma replied. “We all die.” {043-J01}
## Real, not reasonable
Shah’s offering was a Cold War tale. In the 1950s, he said, the CIA wanted to watch China’s nuclear tests from a Himalayan summit, with a plutonium battery to power the listening post.
The equipment was lashed to rocks on Nanda Devi as a storm came in. When the climbers returned, it was gone. It has never been found.
“This is your redemptive story,” Varma said.
Shah replied: “The difference between reality and fiction is that reality is not obliged to be reasonable.” {043-C02}
Varma replied with true history of his own: Delhi between 1803 and 1857, drawn from Swapna Liddle’s *The Broken Script*.

In those fifty years Persian vanished as the language of power, printing presses arrived, and poetry sold newspapers. At Delhi College, Western knowledge was taught in Hindustani. “It’s like we’re teaching the Magna Carta,” Shah said, “but we’re doing it in Urdu.”
## Ships, sheep and vlogs
Shah then told of the German fleet that sat out the First World War in dock and was meant to be delivered to Britain at Scapa Flow. Its sailors blew it up instead.
That raised a question Varma left open: should a soldier obey orders, when we would cheer the same defiance had the sides been reversed? {043-C07}
The wrecks, Shah added, now supply the pre-nuclear steel for Geiger counters, including those that searched Nanda Devi. “The tapestry of the world brings everything together,” he said.

Varma’s last pitch was a low-budget film told only through vlogs, about an everyday vlogger who falls for an androgynous newcomer who seems wholly constructed, and may be the only one being true to themselves.
That set off a debate about authenticity. Shah called it “the laziest pose”. Varma said character is not a rock but a river. {043-C10}
Shah closed with Mussolini’s soldiers in Ethiopia in 1935, who rebelled over bad food and were sent live sheep by parachute. “The sheep is a life support system,” he explained.
Varma called it “the greatest scene of all time”, then signed off with a plea to read good books, fiction or not: “Everything, my friends, is stories.”

second.label: A Soviet side story
second.head: Hot property, cold guard
second.deck: Ajay Shah on a Soviet guard who learned that plutonium is always warm
body: During the Soviet atom bomb project, Ajay Shah said, the physicists were watched by NKVD jailers under Beria, who did not trust them. If the first test failed, the guards had orders to shoot every physicist.

One day a guard burst in on a physicist holding a piece of metal and accused him of passing off stainless steel as plutonium. “You got to be a communist to know the phrase malingerer,” Shah remarked. {043-J05}

The physicist remembered that plutonium is always warm from decay, and sent the guard out into minus twenty degrees holding it. Half an hour later the guard’s earlobes had frostbite. The metal was still warm, and the physicist won a day’s reprieve. {043-S03}

quote.text: Okay, fine, then I’ll kill you tomorrow.

second.caption: the guard who held plutonium

third.head: All the news fit to rhyme
body: What did every Delhi newspaper need in order to sell, Amit Varma asked. Ajay Shah guessed gossip and celebrity scandal. The answer, in Delhi then, was poetry. {043-S07}

“Poets, in a sense, were the great public figures of their time,” Varma said. One typical issue of the *Delhi Urdu Akhbar* carried news from as far afield as Afghanistan, France and Russia. In 1841 it ran an editorial arguing for widow remarriage. {#widow}

Mushairas were everywhere, and the verses recited at them were printed as tazkiras. These sold so well that one Karimuddin, who did not care for poetry, began holding regular mushairas just so he could publish them.
Another tazkira opened with an essay teaching readers what metre is and how to use a metaphor. Early English newspapers, Varma noted, were gossip and tabloid material.
third.caption: poetry that sold newspapers

p2.title: Morals of the story
p2.deck: Each pitch hid an argument: about tests, truth, language, duty and the self

sections.label: The first film
sections.head: The lane less travelled
sections.caption: the boy who left his lane
body: Amit Varma’s first story began with a thought experiment from Deepak VS, a Bangalore entrepreneur in his mid-twenties. Replace the IIT entrance test with a swimming test, Deepak said, and the engineers would be just as good.

Varma got carried away and said they would be better, since what the exam really selects for is “hunger, passion, initiative”. Deepak, “like a wise man, even though he is a young man”, corrected him. By the second year the system would be gamed again, with Kota running swimming classes and billboards of coaches in Speedos. {043-C01}
## Out past the marker

Varma’s film is set a year or two into the new regime. Its hero has an engineer’s mind but must slog through IIT-sized pools against boys who care nothing for engineering. The person he is falling for reaches across from the next lane and hits him to get ahead.

He escapes to the sea and, for the first time, enjoys swimming. His coaching grades slide, he fails, and his mother stops talking to him. He swims out past the danger marker into a gathering storm. {043-S01}
Ajay Shah found it “deep and allegorical”, unlike “silly TV serials about children preparing in Kota”. {043-J20}
~ Varma closed the chapter with one of his favourite poems, Stevie Smith’s *Not Waving but Drowning*, which ends: “I was much too far out all my life, and not waving but drowning.” {043-R04}

quote.text: To hell with the swimming pool. Why should I stay in my lane?

sections.label: The second film
sections.head: Word soup, every word true
sections.caption: a story that is all true
body: Ajay Shah promised a story with a troubling end in which “every word of it is true”: a CIA plutonium battery lost on Nanda Devi. Then he drew the moral. “The difference between reality and fiction is that reality is not obliged to be reasonable.” {043-C02}

To prove it, he played a pitch meeting with Amit Varma as the movie mogul granting him two minutes. America, India, CIA, China, plutonium, tens of millions at risk in UP, hippies at Nanda Devi: Varma, he said, would call it word soup. {043-J03}
## Still up there

The danger has not passed. One theory, Shah said, is that the battery, always warm from radioactive decay, melted its way hundreds of metres into the glacier and lodged in rock. “The damn thing has a half life of thousands of years,” he said. {#halflife}

Varma was taken with the image of plutonium “sinking, sinking, sinking” through an ice-covered mountain, and with the human drama of the climbers and the government. He also proposed merchandise for the co-producers: a T-shirt reading “Okay, fine, I’ll kill you tomorrow”, the line of a Soviet guard in Shah’s side story. {043-J02}
~ Shah advised listeners to warn their great-great-grandchildren off the Gangetic plain. Varma pointed out that gentle readers do not have great-great-grandchildren.

quote.text: Gentle reader, you should tell your great great grandchildren don’t live in the Gangetic plain.

sections.label: The web series
sections.head: A city loses its language
sections.caption: Delhi in churn, 1803 to 1857
body: Amit Varma’s third pitch was a web series set in Delhi between 1803, when the East India Company won the second Anglo-Maratha war, and 1857. {#maratha} The Mughals ruled in name; the Company held the power.

What gripped him most was something that rarely happens in human history: the lingua franca changed. Persian held the place English holds in India today, “nobody’s mother tongue” but the language of power. Within fifty years it was out.
“If you are a kid who’s ten years old,” he said, “you look at your parents and they’re completely helpless in the new world.” {043-C03}
## Western knowledge, local tongue
Printing presses spread at the same time. “When you write down a word, you ossify it,” Varma said: print brings stability but loses some of the flux of a spontaneous order. {043-C04}

Delhi College’s endowment came from one Fazal Ali, on condition that teaching be in local languages. So Western knowledge was taught in Hindustani, which had no technical terms for it, “a lot of which is a problem to this day”. {043-C05}

~ The cast was full of contradictions. Ghalib, already a legend, ran from a moneylender and tried to suck up to the British. Raja Ram Mohan Roy, a fearless reformer, pleaded with a Mughal emperor in obsequious terms. {043-C06}

quote.text: It seems to me to be a great locus of all this, because you have the collision of the worlds there.

sections.label: The fourth film
sections.head: Return to sender
sections.caption: the navy that was never delivered
body: Ajay Shah asked listeners to imagine an Amazon delivery, then “a delivery of a navy”. {043-J07} Under the Treaty of Versailles, Germany’s freshly minted fleet was to be handed to Britain at Scapa Flow. Its sailors sank it instead.

Amit Varma raised the hard question. A soldier, he said, should follow orders, because “if everyone starts rationalizing like that, you kinda get screwed”. Yet had England lost and the Nazis been taking its navy, we would cheer the soldier who blew it up. {043-C07}
That, Shah said, made it “lovely movie material”: some sailors must have argued that a deal is a deal, others that a navy that had never fought should not be given away.
## A mirror in Algeria
He set it beside Mers-el-Kébir in Algeria, from an earlier episode. There French sailors chose to obey orders rather than join the British, who opened fire. Thousands died.

Then he tied the threads. Since nuclear testing began, nearly all new steel has been contaminated, so Geiger counters need steel made before the bomb, cut by divers from the wrecks at Scapa Flow. The counters that searched Nanda Devi were made of it. {043-S09}
~ Varma called it marvellous. The universe, Shah allowed, would have found some other source, “but it is just so sweet that these stories tie together”.

quote.text: Why the hell will we give a freshly minted navy that has never fought a war?

sections.label: The fifth film
sections.head: When the mask becomes the face
sections.caption: authenticity and love
body: Amit Varma’s fifth pitch was a low-budget film made entirely of vlogs, with no third-person camera. Its showpiece is a vloggers’ Mexican standoff, cameras in place of guns, pulling back into a hall of mirrors. {043-J14}
But, he said, “the crux of the story always has to do with love”. An everyday, likable vlogger falls for a newcomer who seems wholly constructed: beautiful, androgynous, impossible to pin down.

Love, in Iris Murdoch’s words as Varma quoted them, is “the extremely difficult realization that someone other than oneself is real”. We all live with main character syndrome, he said, until love makes someone else real. {043-C11}
Varma wants the viewer to see, in the end, that the androgynous vlogger is the one being true to themselves. How the film gets there, he admitted, he has not thought of yet. {043-J10}
## Without effort
Ajay Shah pressed him on authenticity. “There is only one person that I can be without effort, and that is me,” Shah said, and he defined authenticity as the laziest pose. {043-C09}
~ Varma questioned the word itself. Skip breakfast and the chemistry of the brain shifts by evening. And a pose you keep working at becomes yours: “the mask becomes a face often”.

quote.text: We think my character is a rock. No, it isn’t. My character is a river.

side.boxText: Amit Varma’s Delhi pitch rests on Swapna Liddle’s *The Broken Script*, which he called one of the finest history books he has read in recent years, and the best book of quasi-Mughal history he has come across. {043-R01}

contQuote.text: But you realize that there are different currents that we swim in at the same time. Some are the currents of history, some are the currents of society, and there’s all this other personal stuff happening.

p3.title: Stranger than fiction
p3.deck: Lost plutonium, a sunken fleet, falling sheep and a forgotten mathematician

stories.start: So we are going to take you back to the age when the Chinese
stories.end: Who knows? Plutonium will keep going for thousands of years.
stories.caption: the plutonium lost on Nanda Devi
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah’s Cold War tale from the Himalayas
stories.head: Last seen on Nanda Devi
body: In the 1950s China was on its way to a nuclear weapon, and its tests would naturally take place on the Tibetan plateau. Spy satellites could not yet watch it, Ajay Shah said. So the CIA came to India with a proposition.

An Indian Army team had just climbed Kanchenjunga. The Americans wanted to haul equipment to its summit, “some twenty eight thousand feet high”, and spend years gathering dust from the air and measuring radioactivity over Tibet. {#summit} Power would come from a battery driven by plutonium decay.
The Indian climbers, back from the summit a month earlier, flatly refused. Nobody, they said, could carry a 70-kilogram battery up Kanchenjunga. {#battery} They proposed Nanda Devi instead.

Elite American climbers were approached by the CIA one by one: all expenses paid, total secrecy. On the second attempt, with a storm coming, the team lashed the equipment to rocks at a spot they memorised, since there was no GPS, and ran down. When they returned, the place was unrecognisable and the equipment was gone.
It was never found. If its plutonium ever reached the Ganga, Shah said, tens of millions of people in the Gangetic plain would die. {043-S02}
India needed a cover story. Too many hikers and hippies, it said, were damaging a precious biodiversity reserve. Nanda Devi was shut to all, and for years searched with Geiger counters.
~ One theory is that the Chinese climbed up from their side and took it. Another is that the warm plutonium melted its way hundreds of metres into the glacier, where it sits still.
stories.why: A Cold War spy plan and an environmental closure turned out to be one story. Reality, Shah said, is not obliged to be reasonable, and this one has not ended: the plutonium will keep going for thousands of years. {043-C02}
stories.postscript: Nanda Devi, Shah added, is one of the world’s most glorious hiking regions. Readers who have never hiked must “run, not walk”.

stories.start: I want to take you back to the early 20th century

stories.caption: the scuttling at Scapa Flow
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on a fleet that would not be delivered
stories.head: Sunk costs at Scapa Flow
body: Germany built a navy to challenge the Royal Navy, Ajay Shah said, but in 1914 it was not ready. Its shiny new ships, probably half the size of the British fleet, sat out the First World War in dock. {#halfsize}

The Treaty of Versailles capped the German army at 100,000 men, with no tanks and no navy. {#versailles} More than a hundred ships and more than a hundred submarines were to be delivered to Britain at Scapa Flow, at the top of Scotland.

The German sailors had other plans. They mounted explosives in their ships, and one by one something like seventy or eighty big warships blew up and sank. {043-S08} Many died, because the evacuations had not been planned.
~ In the days before the handover, Shah noted, the sailors had been treated pettily, without enough food or sanitation.

quote.text: You may have signed the treaty of Versailles. We refuse. We’re not giving you the ships.

stories.start: Okay, I'll take you back to 1935. Mussolini had delusions of grandeur.
stories.end: but yes, there is at least one photograph of this.
stories.caption: the parachuting sheep
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah’s scene for the writers of the world
stories.head: Dinner arrives by parachute
body: In 1935, Ajay Shah said, Mussolini had delusions of grandeur. {#mussolini} He meant to recreate the Roman Empire, and led an invasion of what is now Ethiopia and Somalia.

His soldiers were “just guys who wanted to have a good time”. Their hearts were not in the fight, nor were their stomachs, and out in the boondocks groups of them rebelled over bad military food. {043-J11}

The fix: sheep from Italy were loaded onto planes, strapped to parachutes and dropped one by one over the army camps, and a near mutiny was staved off. Why not drop boxes of meat, Amit Varma asked. “The sheep is a life support system,” Shah said. “It has an immune system. It keeps the meat fresh.” {043-S11}
~ At least one photograph survives, Shah said: “a very blurry, bad black and white photo”. {#photo}
stories.why: A near mutiny was averted by solving a food problem, with a fix as absurd as it was workable. Shah offered it as a scene, not a full story, for the world’s writers to build on.

stories.start: There's a great character called Ram Chandar. Have you heard of him?
stories.end: Partly also because of eighteen fifty seven changes everything, but I'll get there.
stories.caption: Ramchandra, the forgotten mathematician
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a genius history mislaid
stories.head: The Ramanujan who missed his Hardy
body: Ramchandra, born in 1821, taught at Delhi College and tried to explain the rules of calculus using algebra. {043-S05}

His treatise reached the British mathematician Augustus De Morgan, who was blown away and tried his best to promote him. Amit Varma recalled a reference calling the pair the Hardy and Ramanujan of their age, except that Hardy succeeded and De Morgan could not.

Ramchandra was also a fearless rationalist. He spoke out against traditional medicine and against every religion, local and Western, and started journal after journal to get his ideas to the people. Then, having just crossed thirty in 1852, he converted to Christianity, which nothing he had written explains. {#convert}
~ After 1857, Varma said, he became “a headmaster of some random school”.
stories.why: Genius alone did not decide who became famous: patronage and the upheaval of 1857 mattered too. And even a well-documented life, Varma found, can stay a mystery, as Ramchandra’s conversion shows.
